subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Euthyphro Dilemma: Does God Decide What's Good?
description: A 60-second lesson on The Euthyphro Dilemma: Does God Decide What's Good?.

hook.text: Plato asked: Is something good because God commands it? Or does God command it because it's good?

buildup.text: Horn 1: if good = whatever God says, then God could command torture and it would be good. Morality becomes arbitrary.

discovery.text: Horn 2: if God commands things because they're already good, then goodness exists independently of God.

twist.text: This 2,400-year-old dilemma still applies to any authority-based ethics: 'It's right because the law says so.' Same.

climax.text: The lesson: morality can't be grounded solely in authority.

punchline.text: If 'good' just means 'whatever the authority says,' then nothing is truly good.

quiz.question: What does the Euthyphro dilemma challenge?
options: The idea that morality can be grounded solely in divine or authoritative command

details.summary: The Euthyphro dilemma asks whether things are good because God commands them, or God commands them because they are good. Either answer creates problems for grounding morality in divine authority.
details.whyItMatters: This ancient puzzle forces anyone who grounds ethics in religion to confront whether morality can exist independently of divine command.
takeaways: If good is whatever God commands, morality becomes arbitrary
If God commands what is independently good, morality is separate from God
The dilemma has persisted for over two thousand years

faq.question: What are the two horns of the Euthyphro dilemma?
faq.answer: Either God's commands make things good (making morality arbitrary) or things are good independently and God merely recognizes them (making God unnecessary for ethics).

faq.question: How do religious thinkers respond to the Euthyphro dilemma?
faq.answer: Many argue that goodness flows from God's nature rather than arbitrary commands, attempting a middle path that grounds morality in divine character rather than will.
